theme: Water · Victoria: radar checked against clear optical images
title: Sale Common wetland, Victoria: water rising, then receding
place: 6 km window around Sale Common Nature Conservation Reserve, Gippsland, Victoria, Australia. The window is not the park boundary
product: NISAR L2 GCOV, L-band, Frequency A, HHHH and HVHV, 20 m
task: A wetland manager wants to know where water spread and where it drained between two satellite passes, to plan checks on the ground.
optical_text: Sentinel-2 optical images on 28 September, 8 October and 18 October, screened for cloud, shadow and image edges. From these alone, 100 m cells were labelled as new water, water lost, or stable land before any radar value was read. Switch on the 8 October optical image in the map layers to compare.
agreement: Yes, on these labelled cells. With the rule 'HV drops by at least 3 dB', 64% of the 276 cells the optical images call new water pass, and 4% of the 1550 stable-land cells. If the threshold is set so that about 5% of stable land passes (2.4 dB), 72% of new water passes. Cells that lost water brightened again. These are group results over many cells, not the value at a point you click, and new water and water lost are different cells. The optical and radar dates differ by 8 to 56 hours.

what_happened: Parks Victoria reports Sale Common partly closed from 16 October 2026 because of flooding. Sentinel-2 optical images show water spreading across the wetland between 28 September and 8 October and shrinking again by 18 October. The closure date is not the day the flooding began.

sources.label: Parks Victoria: Sale Common Nature Conservation Reserve
Geoscience Australia, Digital Earth Australia Sentinel-2 analysis-ready data

radar_summary: Cells that the optical images show turning into water darkened by about 3.7 dB in HH and 4.2 dB in HV, while stable land moved by less than 0.4 dB. Cells that lost their water brightened again by 2.3 dB in HH and 3.5 dB in HV. There are three radar dates. 8 October is the middle pass and the date of the largest water area in the optical images; three passes cannot show the exact day of the peak or when the water began to fall.
class_table_note: Groups are 100 m cells labelled from Sentinel-2 alone (water fraction of at least 0.8, with cloud, shadow and edge screening), chosen without looking at the radar. Values are the median radar change in each group. Cell counts are the cells that passed screening, not a flooded area.
mechanism: Candidate explanation: where land turns into smooth open water, the radar energy reflects away from the satellite and the return drops. When the water goes, wet ground and plants are exposed and the return rises again. Both polarisations show it here, HV a little more strongly.

independent_evidence.question: Is there independent evidence of the change?
independent_evidence.text: Water and land labels come from Sentinel-2 optical images and were fixed before looking at the radar.

reference_extent.question: Is there ground truth to test against?
reference_extent.text: No ground survey, water levels or official flood extent. Optical labels are not ground truth.

limits: The optical images and radar passes are 8 to 56 hours apart, so the water can have moved in between.
Water that stayed water also changed (HH about -2.9 dB in the second interval), so wind and surface roughness affect the radar return as well.
There is no accuracy assessment and no comparison of matched land-cover types.
The window includes town, farmland and river as well as wetland.
This tests how the radar responds on existing optical labels. It does not validate an automatic radar flood map, and it does not show water under trees.
use_for: Screening where a wetland is filling or draining between 12-day passes, so managers can decide where to check on the ground.
A starting point for following wetland water on cloudy days. That use still needs testing against clear days like these.
not_for: It is not a flood extent or water depth product.
It is not evidence that radar detects water under forest.
tour: Sale Common wetland, Victoria, on the 8 Oct optical image. Purple cells: where the radar return dropped by at least 3 dB in HV between 26 Sep and 8 Oct. They sit on the water that spread across the wetland.
Now the radar change map itself. Left of the line: change from 26 Sep to 8 Oct, while the water spread. Right: 8 to 20 Oct, while it receded. Blue is darker, red is brighter.
This is HV. On cells that optical images show turning into water, HH fell 3.7 dB and HV 4.2 dB. Stable land moved less than 0.4 dB.
Under the map, drag the threshold: the panel shows how many optical new-water cells and how many stable-land cells pass the rule. Then download the cells that pass.
Your turn: change the rule, click a cell, download the cells that pass, or open another case.
headline: Cells that optical images show turning into water darkened by a median 4.2 dB in HV, while stable land moved less than 0.4 dB. A rule that flags 5% of stable land selects 72% of the new-water cells.
